title: The ragas close
hook: the walk through the Granth's ragas ends: dusk, dawn, spring, rain and a serious morning, all carrying one Word

segments.voice: Yesterday, your raga, and Guru Amar Das's line that a raga stands high if it brings love for the True One. Your line was my raga. Which one did you name? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-one.

Watch one river from the same bridge all day. Gray and quick at dawn. Brown and slow at noon. Gold at evening, then black, with lights on it. Someone passing at each hour could think it was a different river. It's one water, wearing the hours. That's where this block of the path ends. Since the day we asked why the Granth is sung, we've walked raga by raga through its pages. Today the ragas close, and we look at what ran through all of them.
screen: `ONE RIVER, CHANGING ALL DAY.` → `ONE WATER, WEARING THE HOURS.` → `WHAT RAN THROUGH ALL OF THEM?`

segments.voice: Look back at the road. We began with why the Granth is sung at all, then the small markings, ghar and rahao, then strings and drums, then the order of the ragas. Then Sri Rag, Majh, Gauri, Asa, and on through the book: Sorath and Bilaval, Ramkali and Maru, Tukhari's months, Kedara's dusk, Bhairao's serious morning, Basant's spring, Malar's rain, Kanara, Kalyan's evening, Prabhati's dawn, and Jaijavanti, where the ragas end. Then the Ragmala, held with respect in two ways, the ragis who keep the old tunes alive, and yesterday, the raga that feels like yours. Each of those sections opens under its own heading, with an invocation of the One. Every one holds hymns that point the same way: toward the Name, the Word, the Shabad. The moods changed. The Word didn't. Guru Nanak has a line in the Japji that fits the whole block. In paraphrase: with a single word, the Creator spread out the expanse of creation, and from it rivers beyond counting flowed. One word; many rivers. That's the shape of the ragas, too. The Gurus didn't write a different faith for the morning and another for the evening. They set the one Word in mood after mood, so it could meet a person wherever they happened to be: tender at dusk, hopeful in spring, heavy-hearted on a hard morning, quiet before dawn. So when you hear kirtan from now on, the raga name at the top isn't a puzzle to solve. It's the hour the Word has dressed for. Tomorrow, a new block: Guru Nanak's longer teachings, starting with a conversation on a mountain, recorded in Ramkali. Your line: many moods, one word.
screen: `FROM WHY IT'S SUNG TO JAIJAVANTI.` · `EVERY SECTION POINTS TO THE NAME.` · `ONE WORD, MANY RIVERS.` · `THE HOUR THE WORD HAS DRESSED FOR.` · then, large: `MANY MOODS, ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to a new raga today. If you can, pick one raga we didn't linger on, or one you skipped, and play a shabad sung in it. Let it be unfamiliar. Then sit. Notice the mood it brings, without naming it too fast: bright, heavy, longing, still. Then, under the mood, listen for the steady thing: the breath going in and out, the same as it was in every other raga. If you pray, you can let the Word, Waheguru, be the river under the changing light. If you don't, let the breath be that river, one water through every hour. The bell holds the time.
The ragas close. The end of our walk through the Granth's ragas, where every section, in every mood, points to one Word. Today's word.
Your line: many moods, one word. Today, as your own moods shift, morning to evening, notice one thing about you that stays the same through all of them. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear the Granth's ragas in kirtan through the day and the year, with different ragas for different hours and seasons, all of them carrying Gurbani, the Guru's Word.

trapdoor: what you thought: the ragas are many separate songs.
what it means: the Gurus set one Word in many moods, so it could meet people at every hour.
what a scholar hears: Japji 16 pictures creation spreading out from a single word, with rivers flowing from it: one source, many streams.
